passage: The review meeting at the ward office ended, and Hemant sat back down with the composting report open. 'Total flop,' he muttered. Omkar, from the accounts desk, pulled up a chair. 'Flop out of ten, or flop out of what?' Hemant almost laughed. On the whiteboard he drew a line from 0 to 10. Collection from the two big colonies: steady every week, so maybe a 7. Bins in the market lane: broken twice, smelly, a 3. Volunteer turnout: strong for a month, then gone, a 4. He wrote two columns, Kept Going and Fell Apart, and the second was shorter than he expected. 'So it's a five, not a zero,' Omkar said. Hemant circled the market lane. 'And this is what the next round fixes first.'

qa.a: The bins in the market lane, which broke twice and were smelly, got a 3.

qa.q: Why did 'total flop' feel true to Hemant right after the review meeting?
qa.a: The problems were the loudest thing in his mind after the meeting, so one bad part seemed to stand for the whole drive. A single verdict also spared him the work of sorting through the details.

qa.q: What choice turned Hemant's review from a verdict into a plan?
qa.a: Drawing a 0-to-10 line and making two columns let him score each part on its own, so he could see the colonies were working and pick the market lane as the first fix.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Hemant's shift from 'flop' to 'five'?
qa.a: Omkar likely finds this far more useful: a flat 'flop' gave the team nothing to act on, while a five with one clear first fix gives everyone a next step.

Love,
Lalremsiami

grounding: Shows a young woman writing down her fear of losing a new job, what she would do and how likely it is, and deciding to go anyway.

passage:
Note for Trisha's parents, Thursday
Trisha came in quiet today and didn't want her snack. When I asked, she said the class play list went up and her name wasn't on it. Then she said, very flatly, 'Mrs Pillai thinks I'm useless. She doesn't like me.' I asked how she knew. 'I just know. She looked at me when she read the names.' She said it three times, like something already checked. I didn't argue. I asked what else Mrs Pillai had said to her this week, and she remembered a 'good work' on her map. She went quiet at that. I suggested she ask Mrs Pillai about backstage jobs tomorrow, and she is thinking about it. You may want to talk it through tonight.
Deepika, after-school centre

qa.q: What did Trisha remember Mrs Pillai writing this week?
qa.a: Trisha remembered a 'good work' on her map.

qa.q: Why does 'Mrs Pillai thinks I'm useless' feel like a fact to Trisha?
qa.a: Trisha is hurt at being left off the list, and one look while the names were read seems to explain it; the hurt makes a guess feel as certain as something she was told.

qa.q: Which of Deepika's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Deepika didn't argue but asked what else Mrs Pillai had said, which let Trisha find a real piece of evidence, the 'good work', that didn't fit the belief.

qa.q: How might Mrs Pillai feel if she learned what Trisha believed?
qa.a: Mrs Pillai would likely be surprised and sorry, since she had praised Trisha's map that same week and may have had many reasons for the play list.

grounding: Shows a child left off a play list stating as fact that her teacher thinks she is useless, based only on a look.

passage:
Tuesday
Dear Diary,
Sir put up the list for the Annual Day play and I am NOT on it. Noor is the queen. Even Bilal got the lion and he can't remember lines. So now it is clear. Sir thinks I'm useless. He never smiles at me. Yesterday he said 'sit properly, Hafsa' and he didn't say it to anyone else. That proves it. Noor said maybe there are only eight parts and Sir chose the tall ones for the costumes, but Noor doesn't understand. I KNOW what he thinks. I am not putting my hand up in his class ever again. I didn't even eat Ammi's kheer tonight.
Hafsa

qa.q: Which part did Noor get in the play?
qa.a: Noor is the queen.

qa.q: Why does 'sit properly, Hafsa' feel like proof to Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa is hurt about the list and is hunting for a reason 😔, so an ordinary reminder looks like a sign of dislike, and the belief feels true without any real evidence.

qa.q: What could help Hafsa before deciding never to raise a hand again?
qa.a: Hafsa could ask Sir how the parts were chosen, or check Noor's idea about eight parts and costumes, before treating a guess as fact.

qa.q: How might Noor feel when Hafsa waves away the idea about eight parts?
qa.a: Noor might feel unheard and a little stuck, trying to help a friend who has already decided what Sir thinks.

grounding: Shows a child who was not cast in the play declaring in a diary, without evidence, that the teacher thinks they are useless.

passage: In the small school by the paddy fields outside Thodupuzha, Elizabeth Teacher chalked the names for the Children's Day skit on the board. Salma read them twice. Her name wasn't there. On the walk home along the canal, she kicked every stone she passed. 'Teacher hates me,' she told Umma at the gate. 'She thinks I'm useless.' 'Did she say so?' 'She doesn't have to. She gave the mango-seller part to Beena, and Beena can't even act.' Umma handed her a glass of water. 'And who reads the prayer every Monday?' Salma looked into the glass. 'Me.' 'Who chose you for that?' Salma didn't answer, but she stopped kicking the gatepost.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth Teacher writing the names for?
qa.a: The names were for the Children's Day skit.

qa.q: What does Salma kicking every stone suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: Salma is hurt and angry at being left out, and she has already turned it into a story that Elizabeth Teacher thinks she is useless, which feels certain to her.

qa.q: What turning point does Umma's question create?
qa.a: Asking who chose Salma to read the prayer puts one real fact against the guess, and Salma's silence shows the belief starting to loosen.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth Teacher see the skit list differently from Salma?
qa.a: Elizabeth Teacher may have chosen parts for many reasons, like giving Beena a turn, and may never have thought of it as a judgement on Salma at all.

grounding: Shows a village schoolgirl left out of a skit announcing as fact that her teacher thinks she is useless, with no evidence.

passage: Second period, Istanbul, the first cold morning of November. Nour had worn her cousin's old green coat because her own had torn at the zip. When she walked in, Selin leaned over to Defne and whispered something, and Defne put a hand over her mouth. That was it. Nour knew exactly what had been said: Look at that coat. Where did she dig that up? She could almost hear Selin's voice saying it. She kept the coat on all through maths so nobody could see it was too big at the shoulders, even though she was sweating. At lunch she ate alone in the library. By evening she had decided never to wear the green coat again. She never asked what the whisper was. She never checked.

qa.q: Why was Nour wearing her cousin's old green coat?
qa.a: Because her own coat had torn at the zip.

qa.q: Why did Nour feel so sure Selin was mocking the coat?
qa.a: Nour already felt self-conscious in a coat that was too big, so when the whisper came her own worry supplied the words, and they felt as real as if she had heard them.

qa.q: What small step could Nour have taken before hiding in the library?
qa.a: Nour could have asked Selin or Defne what was funny, or simply noticed that she hadn't heard a single word, before acting as if she had.

qa.q: What might Selin and Defne actually have been whispering about?
qa.a: They could have been talking about anything, from a teacher to weekend plans; from their side, the coat may never have come up at all.

grounding: Shows a teenager treating classmates' whisper as spoken mockery of her coat, without ever checking what was said.

passage: At the district swimming club, the under-16 group waited by the pool for the coach. Eshaan's trunks were last year's, faded at the back, and he had been tugging at them since the changing room. On the bench, Mridul said something low to the swimmer in the next lane, and they both grinned. Eshaan's face burned. They'd seen the faded patch. Mridul had definitely said, 'Look at his trunks, still in kid size.' Eshaan could hear it as clearly as the whistle. He jumped in before his lane was called and swam the warm-up with his head down. After practice, Mridul called out, 'Eshaan! Did you see Coach's new sunglasses? Total traffic cop!' Eshaan stopped halfway through towelling his hair. Oh.

qa.q: What was wrong with Eshaan's trunks?
qa.a: Eshaan's trunks were last year's, faded at the back.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan 'hear' Mridul's words so clearly?
qa.a: Eshaan had been worried about the faded trunks since the changing room, so when Mridul spoke low, his own worry filled in the words and they sounded real.

qa.q: What could Eshaan try the next time he sees a whisper and a grin?
qa.a: Eshaan could remind himself that he heard nothing, then wait or ask what's funny before spending a whole warm-up with his head down.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel on finding out Eshaan thought the joke was about the trunks?
qa.a: Mridul would probably be surprised and a little sorry, since the joke was about Coach's sunglasses and Mridul wanted to share it with Eshaan.

grounding: Shows a teen swimmer certain that a whispered joke mocked his faded trunks, until the joke turns out to be about the coach.

passage:
Dear Rekha didi,
You said to write when things get bad, so here I am. Today was colour day at school, and I wore the orange salwar suit Mummy stitched, the one with the mirror work. In the corridor Harleen and Jaspreet looked at me, looked at each other, and whispered. I know they were saying it looks homemade. I know Harleen said 'aunty suit'. I didn't hear it, but I know. I spent the rest of the day with my dupatta pulled over the embroidery so nobody could see it. I haven't told Mummy, because she was so proud of it.
Did anyone ever laugh at your clothes? Tell me honestly.
Simran

qa.q: What colour was the salwar suit Simran wore?
qa.a: Simran wore the orange salwar suit.

qa.q: Why does Simran feel so sure about words that were never heard?
qa.a: Simran already worries the suit looks homemade, so the whisper seems to confirm it; that is why Simran can write 'I didn't hear it, but I know' and hide the embroidery all day.

qa.q: What could Rekha didi suggest as a next step?
qa.a: Rekha didi could ask what Simran actually saw and heard, and suggest a friendly word with Harleen or Jaspreet instead of hiding the suit.

qa.q: What would change if Simran told Mummy about the day?
qa.a: Mummy might feel sad that the suit caused worry, but could reassure Simran and help separate what happened from what was imagined.

grounding: Shows a teenager, in a letter, certain that two classmates' whisper mocked a homemade suit though nothing was heard.

passage: The rain had flooded the bus stop outside the college, and the last bus to Thrissur was forty minutes late. Elizabeth had been awake since four for her practical exam; she leaned on the pole with her eyes half closed. Anjali was scrolling through homestay photos. 'Three days in Wayanad after results. Look at this one, it has a swing.' Elizabeth nodded. 'Mm.' 'Fine,' Anjali said, locking the phone. 'You clearly hate the plan. You could just say so.' Elizabeth felt the words land wrong, like a coat on the wrong shoulders. She opened her eyes. 'I don't hate it. I'm so tired I can't feel my face. Show me the swing again tomorrow, when I'm a person?' Anjali looked at her properly, then laughed. 'Okay. Tomorrow.'

qa.q: How late was the last bus to Thrissur?
qa.a: The last bus to Thrissur was forty minutes late.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth feel when Anjali said 'You clearly hate the plan'?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt misread, as if a feeling that wasn't hers had been put on her, because the 'Mm' came from exhaustion, not dislike.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make that turned the moment, and why did it work?
qa.a: Elizabeth opened her eyes and calmly named the real feeling, tiredness, and asked to see the swing tomorrow, which corrected the guess without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might the moment have looked from Anjali's side before Elizabeth explained?
qa.a: Anjali was excited and got only 'Mm' back in the rain, so the flat reply felt like rejection; hearing the real reason let Anjali see Elizabeth clearly again.

grounding: Shows a tired student whose flat reply is read as hating a trip plan, and who gently says she is exhausted, not against it.

passage: On the Delhi Metro back from college, Sunaina had the whole Sunday planned: brunch in Hauz Khas, a photo walk, then an open-mic night. She read it out from her notes. Nandini, who had spent the morning at her part-time tutoring job and the afternoon in the lab, was leaning against the glass, watching the stations blur. 'You're doing that face,' Sunaina said. 'You obviously think it's a terrible plan. Just say it.' Nandini blinked. For a second she wanted to snap back. Instead she took a breath. 'It's not the plan. My head's heavy, and I've been talking to Class 9 kids since seven. Can I say yes to brunch and decide the rest tomorrow?' Sunaina's shoulders dropped. 'Oh. Yeah. Of course.'

qa.q: Where did Nandini spend the morning before the metro ride?
qa.a: Nandini spent the morning at her part-time tutoring job.

qa.q: What was Nandini's first impulse when told she obviously thought it was a terrible plan, and why?
qa.a: Nandini wanted to snap back, because having her own feelings described wrongly after such a long day felt unfair.

qa.q: What made Nandini's reply work?
qa.a: Nandini named what was really going on, a heavy head after teaching since seven, and offered a small yes with the rest decided tomorrow, so Sunaina had something true to respond to.

qa.q: What was it like for Sunaina to hear the real reason?
qa.a: Sunaina's dropped shoulders suggest relief 😊; the quiet face had felt like criticism of her plan, and now it was clearly just tiredness.

grounding: Shows a tired student told she obviously thinks a friend's plan is terrible, who calmly explains she is only worn out.

passage:
'So: fest stall. Momos, fairy lights, and we set up near the gate.' Ira looked up. 'Aadhya?'
'Hm.'
'Hm? That's it?'
'Sorry, what?'
'You've been stirring that chai for five minutes. You hate it. You think momos are boring.'
'I didn't say that.'
'You don't have to. Your face is saying it.'
Aadhya put the spoon down. 'Okay. Can I tell you what my face is actually saying?'
'Go on.'
'It's saying I slept three hours because of the lab record. It's not about momos. I like momos.'
'Really?'
'Really. I'm running on chai. Near the gate is smart, everyone walks past it.'
Ira laughed. 'I had a whole argument ready in my head.'
'Save it for the fairy lights. Those I'm not sure about.'

qa.q: Where did Ira want to set up the fest stall?
qa.a: Ira wanted to set up near the gate.

qa.q: How do you think Aadhya felt on being told 'Your face is saying it'?
qa.a: Aadhya likely felt misread and a bit tired of being spoken for, since the quiet came from three hours of sleep, not from any feeling about momos.

qa.q: What choice did Aadhya make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Aadhya put the spoon down and asked to explain what the face really meant, then gave a clear yes on the spot, so the guess was corrected without a quarrel.

qa.q: What was it like for Ira before Aadhya explained?
qa.a: Ira was already defending the plan inside Ira's own head, reading every stir of the chai as disapproval; the real reason turned an imagined argument into a laugh.

grounding: Shows a sleepy student whose silence is read as dislike of a fest plan and who calmly names the real feeling, tiredness.

passage:
Monday: Ishita replied to Aditi's long project update with one word: 'Noted.' No smiley, no thanks. Aditi reread it on the bus and wrote Ishita's side in her head: she thinks I took over her client, she's complaining to the team lead.
Tuesday: Ishita walked past Aditi's desk without stopping. Aditi spent the evening rehearsing an apology for something she couldn't name, and slept badly.
Wednesday: At the water cooler, Aditi's heart was going fast, but she asked. 'Ishita, is something wrong? Did my update step on your toes?' Ishita looked surprised. 'Your update? No, it was great. My father's in hospital, and I've been answering everything in one word. Sorry.' It took two minutes. Aditi walked back lighter, and a little sad she hadn't asked on Monday.

qa.q: What one word did Ishita reply with on Monday?
qa.a: Ishita replied with one word: 'Noted.'

qa.q: Why is Aditi a little sad she hadn't asked on Monday?
qa.a: Aditi sees that two days of made-up conversations and bad sleep could have been replaced by a two-minute question, and feels sorry not to have known about Ishita's father sooner.

qa.q: What choice on Wednesday broke the pattern?
qa.a: Aditi asked directly, 'Is something wrong?', even with her heart going fast, which swapped guessing for a real answer.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt about being asked?
qa.a: Ishita might feel relieved to explain the short replies and grateful that Aditi checked instead of turning cold 🙏.

grounding: Shows a young professional who spends days imagining a colleague's annoyance, then asks directly and learns the real reason in two minutes.

passage: Kamal, you keep looking at Dinesh sir's cabin as if it might bite. Let me tell you something from when I was about your age. My first manager, Mrs Lobo, stopped greeting me in the mornings. Just stopped. For a whole week I built the case in my head: she'd seen my typo in the tender, she'd heard me joke in the lift, she was going to move me to records. I had whole conversations with her in the shower, both sides. I was very good at her lines. On the Friday I was so tired of it that I knocked on her door and asked, 'Have I done something wrong?' She looked up. 'Arohi, no! I've got new glasses and can't see anyone past three feet.' Two minutes. A week of my life. So go and knock.

qa.q: What reason did Mrs Lobo give for not greeting Arohi?
qa.a: Mrs Lobo had new glasses and couldn't see anyone past three feet.

qa.q: Why did the imagined conversations feel so convincing to Arohi?
qa.a: Arohi had real details to hang them on, the typo and the lift joke, and played both sides so often that the imagined lines began to feel like things actually said 😅.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Arohi's story, and what does it suggest for Kamal?
qa.a: The turning point was knocking and asking 'Have I done something wrong?'; it suggests Kamal can end the guessing about Dinesh sir with one direct question.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel after hearing that a week of worry ended in two minutes?
qa.a: Kamal may feel braver and a little amused, seeing that a senior colleague once lived inside a made-up story and got out simply by asking.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague recalling a week of imagined conflict with a manager that one direct question resolved in two minutes.

passage: The monsoon had knocked out Anjali's broadband twice that morning, and she was on her phone's hotspot, one bar, when she noticed Joseph had turned his camera off again. Third call in a row. His messages had shrunk too: 'ok', 'will check'. She had missed the Tuesday review because of the power cut, and by now the story was fixed: he thought she was unreliable, he had already told the client. She spent her lunch break drafting a long explanation. Then she deleted it and typed: 'Joseph, quick one. Are you annoyed with me about Tuesday? I'd rather ask than guess.' The reply came in a minute. 'Annoyed? No! Camera's off because my toddler keeps climbing on me. Sorry for the short replies, typing one-handed 😅' Anjali laughed out loud, alone in her flat.

qa.q: Why was Joseph's camera off?
qa.a: Because the toddler keeps climbing on Joseph.

qa.q: Why did Anjali's story about Joseph feel so fixed by lunchtime?
qa.a: Anjali already felt guilty about missing the Tuesday review, so the camera and the short messages seemed to confirm what she feared he thought of her.

qa.q: Which choice saved Anjali the most time and worry?
qa.a: Deleting the long explanation and sending one short, direct question, because it got a real answer in a minute instead of more guessing.

qa.q: If Anjali had sent the long explanation instead, how might Joseph have reacted?
qa.a: Joseph might have been confused by a defence against something he never felt, and the chat could have become more awkward rather than clearer.

grounding: Shows a remote worker on a weak connection who is sure a colleague is annoyed, then asks directly and learns the real reason.
